news.title: Letter: Troy Jackson would be a sorry replacement for Susan Collins
Susan Collins' disastrous debate gaffe revealed she was 'in on the lie': ex-GOP operative
news.description: Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) insists Brett Kavanaugh never lied to her about Roe v. Wade, and an ex-GOP strategist thinks he knows why. Former Republican strategist Steve Schmidt seized on the exchange in a Wednesday episode of "The Warning," a day after Collins faced Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in a debate . The moderator asked Collins whether Kavanaugh, who called Roe "settled law" before his confirmation vote, had lied to her. "I do not feel that he lied, but I think that he should not have said it was settled law because to me that meant that it would not be overturned," Collins answered. "But to be fair, you cannot ask a nominee how he might vote on some hypothetical future case." Schmidt said that was the rare moment Collins told the truth. "And that, for once, from the hand-wringing, letter-writing Susan Collins, is the truth," Schmidt said. "Because she was in on the lie." He argued Collins and Kavanaugh "had the same fundamental position" and that the senator's "entire public legacy" now rests on ending a right American women would still have if she had lost a race in time. Schmidt contrasted Collins with Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine Republican senator remembered for standing on principle during a dangerous era. Collins, he said, is the "complete opposite." "She's a kneeling MAGA sycophant who appeased a fascist for power, who sold out her people, her state, her country, and betrayed her oath, and is addicted to her Senate seat like a junkie in the street," Schmidt said. He also mocked Collins for touting her success in getting "concrete, pulp, and road salt removed from the tariff list," summing up her pitch as "let them eat rock salt." Jackson made the same point onstage, telling voters, "We can't eat road salt." Jackson also compared Collins to "an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out," noting she votes with President Donald Trump 96 percent of the time. "It doesn't matter if she stands with him in public," Schmidt said. "She stands with him in the back room, and everybody knows it." He added, "Mainers, vote her out."

news.title: Susan Collins' debate blunder baffles MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace: 'Ripe for SNL mockery'
news.description: Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) walked into a trap at her Senate debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, bragging about how she got road salt exempted from President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada, only for Jackson to point out that she's just chipping around the edges at a policy broadly hurting Maine and that "we can't eat road salt." The moment left MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace astounded — and she was quick to analyze it alongside correspondent John Heilemann. "I was a staffer, and so I'm sure a staffer was involved," said Wallace, noting that congressional staffers have had a bad couple of weeks with the Eric Schmitt incident . "This is a staffer who was told to go find something that Susan Collins was helpful with. And so someone said, I got one, I got one. They ... went to AI [and asked] 'Is there anything that we've made cheaper?' And they found one. They found road salt." This was obviously going to backfire, said Wallace: "This is ripe for an SNL mockery. People are struggling to put gas in their car. Truckers are struggling to put diesel in their car. People are struggling to buy groceries. They were already more expensive in Maine. And you're going to tell people the road salt is cheaper. What?" Heilemann agreed, calling it basic campaign malpractice. "She slipped ... in terms of her political instincts," he said. Nor was it her only slip, said Heilemann, who noted that the defense of her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh was also weak. Despite all of this, he noted, the race remains highly close, at a moment when Democrats are polling better in red states like Alaska and Ohio. "It's closer than it would be, I think, if Troy Jackson had been the nominee throughout, if he had run in the primary," rather than replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner, he said. "He's the Kamala Harris of this race. He had to come in late." - YouTube www.youtube.com

news.description: Daily Audio Newscast Afternoon Update - October 7, 2026 mps-post Wed, 10/07/2026 - 14:59 Image (Public News Service) News from around the nation. Audio file Collins and Jackson face off in Maine’s first Senate debate, the Trump administration's immigration policies are linked to increased psychological harm in US children, and drought conditions and rising fuel costs could impact Mississippi's waterfowl hunting season. Transcript The Public News Service Wednesday afternoon update. I'm Mike Clifford. It was the first debate ahead of midterms in the pivotal state of Maine. On Tuesday night, the longtime incumbent Susan Collins clashed with her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. The New York Times notes Jackson repeatedly attacked Collins over her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade. Jackson accused her of not pushing back strongly enough against Trump's agenda. He said, would you trust her to select the next Supreme Court justice? Collins defended her record, saying, I have been the most outspoken opponent of tariffs with Canada. Canada is not China. It is our neighbor, our friend, our closest ally, and our biggest trading partner. Collins added, I've been working behind the scenes and was successful in getting concrete pulp and rolled salt removed from the tariff list. Meantime, groups that help immigrant families are speaking out against the Trump administration's policies, calling them a comprehensive assault on children's well-being. The Trump administration says it has deported more than 605,000 undocumented people since 2025. According to reporting from KFF Health News, data show that one in four American children lives with an immigrant parent and that more than 205,000 U.S.-born children have seen at least one parent detained by immigration authorities since President Trump returned to office. Norma Gomez with the Mixteco Indígena Community Organizing Project in Ventura County says many kids are living in fear. Kids are hurting because either they've lost their father or mother or both. I'm Suzanne Potter. Credit goes to Claudia Boyd-Barnett for original reporting on this story for KFF Health News. And conservationists in Mississippi say drought conditions, rising fuel costs, and fewer farmers planting rice in the state could have an impact on this year's waterfowl hunting season. During the winter months, farmers and landowners typically flood their harvested rice fields to attract migratory birds. The Mississippi Flyway is one of the busiest bird migration corridors in North America, Ryan Delaney with the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership says many rice farmers have filed for bankruptcy and rice production in the state has decreased from several hundred thousand acres to just around 100,000 acres. We have concerns that we would not be able to support as much waterfowl habitat this year and that would limit the amount of opportunities potentially for duck hunters to experience quality hunts. I'm Freda Ross reporting. Next to Florida on a farm in Hardy County where dead citrus trees are subjected to high heat and out comes biochar, a black charcoal-like substance that holds water and nutrients that can be worked back into the soil. Zach Farr is the president of Biotech Applied Research, the non-profit behind the project. For every acre of citrus trees, we're emitting about 11 tons of CO2 when we burn them. That CO2 does have carbon that we could use, so rather than burn the carbon, we can store that carbon. The live demonstration is for Volo Foundation's Florida Climate Week. This is Public News Service. A regulatory case in Minnesota is drawing a lot of attention. It's related to tribal sovereignty and the pursuit of clean energy. The Public Utilities Commission recently found that Minnesota Valley Cooperative Light and Power Association acted unlawfully by threatening to disconnect the Upper Sioux community over its behind-the-meter solar and battery project. Despite the outcome, Hudson Kingston, with the rule-focused group Cure, says a leftover issue is whether tribal governments have the right to switch utilities. He says the commission didn't make a call on that question. It's very unfortunate because utilities are risk-averse, and without that sort of clear certainty, there is ambiguity. He suggests that could make it harder for all of Minnesota's tribal governments wanting to pursue renewables and still partner with a receptive utility. Kingston also expects the PUC outcome to be challenged by the cooperative. I'm Mike Moen. And ICE agents arrested more than 400 people in Indiana last month. Many Hoosiers question if the agents will appear at polling sites in the state and across the country at the midterms. Speaking on an American community media panel recently, some voting rights activists representing Asian, indigenous, black, and Hispanic populations discussed President Donald Trump's hints of placing ICE agents and military personnel at voting locations near or in their neighborhoods. President and executive director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice John Yang says he does not want to minimize voters' uneasiness and says there are ways voters can respond if encountered by an ICE agent. One of the things that generally you can do is just simply ask, am I being detained? I am being stopped for some reason. And unless they give you a clear reason for being stopped, you can always ask, am I free to go? I'm Terry Dee reporting. Finally, Colorado voters get to decide whether the state constitution should be amended to prioritize hunting over all other wildlife management tools. Proponents of Amendment 83 on the November ballot say it would protect hunting rights, a practice integral to the state's heritage, cultural identity, and economy. Aubyn Royal, with the Humane World for Animals Colorado chapter, says she's especially alarmed by the measure's explicit protection of traditional methods. She says if passed, it would be much harder to restrict trophy hunting, bear baiting, trapping, or chasing wildlife with dogs. These practices do cause suffering to wildlife, and in some cases, Colorado voters have already outlawed these practices as unsupporting and unethical. A right to hunt should never become a constitutional shield for cruelty. Supporters maintain that the right to hunt and fish should not be subject to any future laws, ballot initiatives, or Wildlife Commission preferences. I'm Eric Galatas. news.title: Susan Collins' debate-stage excuses for corruption scandal dismantled by reporter
news.description: ProPublica reporter Molly Redden spent Wednesday morning taking apart the defenses Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) offered Tuesday night in her Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, calling several of them inaccurate or misleading. The dispute centers on ProPublica's reporting that the FBI was investigating whether Collins and her staff took part in a bribery scheme, an inquiry that fizzled after President Donald Trump's Justice Department gutted the bureau's ranks. The story rests on Martin Kao, a former government contractor facing prison who told agents he traded campaign donations for overvalued or worthless military contracts. Agents corroborated parts of his account and opened an investigation. Collins pointed to a photo in the debate showing her with Kao at a meeting "months before there was ever a contribution." Her campaign has since released it. But Redden said that doesn't contradict the story, which reports Kao's claim that Collins wanted a donation commitment before meeting. The photo shows a February 2018 meeting, and Kao gave $4,000 that June. Kao declined an interview, so what he agreed to isn't clear, but Redden noted that in politics money is often promised first and paid later. She added that Collins hasn't addressed a bigger episode in 2019. Kao told investigators a top Collins fundraiser asked him for a large donation, and he gave $150,000. Two months later, Redden said, he emailed colleagues saying Collins had promised $32 million in new funding. Collins also repeated her earlier claim that Biden's DOJ thoroughly investigated Kao and found his allegations false. Redden said the investigation at the heart of the story ended in 2025 under Trump and reached no conclusions. According to ProPublica, the agents working it were purged for having worked on cases Trump disliked, leaving no one to carry it forward. Redden also took aim at campaign manager Steve Abbott's claims at a Tuesday event. He said Kao shopped the story to the FBI and "They didn't buy it." Redden said agents actually sifted through hundreds of thousands of documents to corroborate Kao and pushed for a full investigation. When Abbott accused ProPublica of swallowing Kao's account whole, she said reporters did no such thing. They reviewed evidence the FBI collected and interviewed dozens of people before publishing. "Then we published the receipts," Redden wrote. Collins has called the story a political hit job. Her campaign says it was never the target of any investigation and cooperated fully.
